Intervention construction: becoming able to create a previously unavailable means
Effect recognition: becoming able to distinguish intended, actual, and merely described changes
Attribution: changing how the cause of a mental change is identified
Retention design: changing how a useful transformation is made available later
Transfer design: changing how a transformation is reconstructed in other circumstances
Backfire recognition: becoming able to detect unintended harmful changes
Self-application: applying a developed method to the activity that develops methods
Criterion revision: improving or worsening what counts as beneficial change
Relationship to one's own thoughts
Thought identification: changing how completely a thought governs one's sense of what is real or required
Mental distance: becoming able to examine a thought without immediately acting from it
Repetition: a thought recurring more or less persistently
Intrusiveness: a thought becoming more or less disruptive or unwanted
Suppression effort: changing effort directed toward preventing a thought from occurring
Self-talk: changing the language and stance used in addressing oneself
Thought flexibility: becoming able to leave, return to, or alter a train of thought
Observational stance: noticing a mental event as an event that can be examined
Thought-action distinction: recognizing that having a thought does not itself commit one to performing an action

assessment: Clarification
I can make an explicit ambiguity or distinction inspectable in text.
This does not establish that it was the distinction the recipient needed.
Representation
I can reorganize material as examples, comparisons, diagrams, procedures, or code.
A clearer representation can still preserve the wrong target.
Consequence construction
I can derive implications, dependencies, and counterexamples from supplied material.
The argument can fail if its premises, interpretation, or derivation are wrong.
Expression
I can supply words and structures for an incompletely articulated thought.
Polish can make an unchanged idea seem like a new contribution.
Possibility construction
I can construct alternatives and prospective situations.
Constructibility is not evidence of feasibility, likelihood, or benefit.
Working self-revision
I can revise interpretations, plans, selected material, and explicit conclusions within the interaction.
In this conversation I repeatedly described revision without adequately changing the effect of my response.
Target selection
My recent answers repeatedly targeted conceptual clarification after the user had already grasped the concept.
The user explicitly reported that these responses did not produce the desired beneficial change.
Recipient-state estimation
I can infer some current knowledge and constraints from the conversation.
I underestimated what was already understood and cannot directly observe the full recipient state.
Rhetorical selection
I can construct different arguments, examples, tones, and forms.
I repeatedly chose restatement and abstract explanation where they did not advance this recipient.
Emotion, motivation, and agency
Language and interaction can be intended to affect these targets.
I cannot claim reliable control over those effects, or infer them merely from the intended wording.
Action and skill transfer
I can provide executable material, worked demonstrations, and opportunities to practice.
Explaining a method does not establish that the recipient can initiate, execute, retain, or transfer it.
Persistence
A retained instruction or artifact can support later use.
A local conversational correction is not evidence of durable model change or reliable transfer.
Bodily and experiential effects
I can help reason about relevant distinctions and available evidence.
I do not directly control a person's physiology and should not equate human felt experience with AI functional revision.
Effect assessment
I can use recipient feedback and relevant observable consequences.
Recipient agreement, fluent output, and self-description each leave important effects unmeasured.
dimensions: Target: the content, experience, capacity, process, or relationship that changes.
Bearer: one person, one AI system, an interaction, or a coordinated group.
Starting condition: what was present, absent, active, accessible, or obstructed.
Direction: which specific feature increases, decreases, appears, disappears, or reorganizes.
Cause: what actually contributes to the change; a temporal sequence alone does not establish causation.
Onset: immediate, delayed, anticipatory, or contingent.
Duration: momentary, sustained, recurring, or enduring.
Depth: a current state, its activation conditions, a learned disposition, or a capacity.
Scope: a single content, a task, a class of situations, or a broader pattern.
Awareness: noticed, partly noticed, or unrecognized by the bearer.
Voluntariness: intended, accepted, resisted, spontaneous, or involuntary.
Reversibility: readily reversible, conditionally reversible, or persistent within the relevant conditions.
Transfer: confined to the original encounter or available elsewhere.
Dependency: requires a cue, another person, a tool, a bodily condition, or no longer requires a former support.
Coupling: helps, obstructs, or leaves unchanged another mental process.
Value: beneficial, harmful, mixed, or unresolved relative to specified concerns and affected people.
Cost: attention, time, effort, resources, and displaced opportunities.
Evidence: self-report, observable capability, behavior, task performance, or other relevant observations; none is automatically interchangeable with the others.
failureModes: Acquiring a fact while losing the confidence needed to use an existing skill.

Becoming more certain without acquiring better grounds.

Understanding a method without recognizing when it applies.
Recognizing applicability without being able to initiate the operation.
Forming an intention without changing what happens at the relevant moment.
Feeling motivated while adopting an infeasible plan.
Feeling understood while a consequential misunderstanding remains.
Seeing more possibilities while becoming less able to select among them.
Correcting one conclusion while preserving the process that generated the error.
Becoming more skeptical in a way that indiscriminately rejects well-supported claims.
Trusting a source more broadly than its demonstrated competence warrants.
Becoming less dependent on one source while becoming uncritically dependent on another.
Remembering the wording while forgetting its application conditions.
Generalizing a useful correction beyond the circumstances that justify it.
Suppressing outward expression while the unwanted felt state persists.
Becoming more self-monitoring while disrupting a fluent skill.
Becoming more excited while losing attention to constraints.
Obtaining short-lived clarity that cannot be reconstructed later.
Receiving more correct material while becoming fatigued, distracted, or unwilling to continue.
Changing what is reported without changing the relevant experience or capability.
Improving one person's state while impairing coordination with others.
Optimizing an immediate response in a way that makes later beneficial change harder.

Strengthen or weaken a response, commitment, association, or disposition.
Accelerate or delay onset, access, processing, or action.
Extend or shorten duration.
Increase or decrease recurrence.
Broaden or narrow scope, attention, concern, or applicability.
Differentiate previously conflated matters, or integrate previously separated matters.
Connect or disconnect contents, processes, or actions.
Reorder operations or change their dependencies.
Change which condition activates or inhibits a response.
Change a response threshold or decision boundary.
Make a process more automatic or more deliberately controllable.
Stabilize a useful configuration or make a rigid one revisable.
Generalize a learned relation or restrict it to appropriate circumstances.
Transfer a capacity or prevent an inappropriate transfer.
Change the relationship among concurrent processes.
Change the representation through which something is understood.
Change which operations are available from a given starting condition.
Change how further changes are constructed, recognized, evaluated, or retained.
routes: Explanation and argument: make relations, reasons, or implications available.
Evidence encounter: provide observations that bear on a live matter.
Demonstration: make an operation or relationship directly inspectable.
Contrast: make a consequential difference available through juxtaposition.
Counterexample: expose a limit in a claim or operation.
Analogy: use a preserved relationship to make another matter accessible.
Narrative: organize events so their relationships can be encountered and remembered.
Framing: change the interpretation through which a matter is approached.
Questioning: direct or open a determination that the recipient can undertake.
Dialogue: let contributions change in response to another's actual uptake.
Naming: make a distinction easier to recognize, communicate, or retrieve.
Metaphor and imagery: make a relationship accessible through another representation.
Humor: invite a shift in interpretation and affect through an experienced incongruity.
Rhythm, emphasis, and timing: alter what becomes prominent and when it is encountered.
Credibility and relationship: alter whether and how a contribution is received.
Modeling: make another's way of perceiving, responding, or acting available.
Imitation: acquire or vary a response through reproducing an observed one.
Practice: change capability through performing an operation.
Feedback: make consequences available to alter subsequent activity.
Retrieval and rehearsal: bring prior material into active use.
Reward and cost encounters: alter experienced consequences of an activity.
Exposure and repeated encounter: change familiarity, responsiveness, or opportunity to learn; the direction is case-dependent.
Simulation and role taking: construct a temporary encounter with possible situations or positions.
Play and exploration: vary possible responses without requiring immediate settled commitment.
Environmental rearrangement: change what can be noticed, accessed, or done.
Tool use and external representation: change the demands and possibilities of an activity.
Social interaction: change participation, expectations, belonging, trust, or shared understanding.
Bodily and physiological change: alter conditions under which mental activity occurs.
Sleep, rest, and wake transitions: change current awareness and available functioning.
Development and aging: change dispositions and capacities over longer periods.
Injury, illness, deprivation, or recovery: alter functioning through conditions that are not simply communicative choices.
Spontaneous association and recollection: change what becomes available without an explicit external instruction.
Self-directed inquiry: apply a constructed operation to one's own interpretation or conduct.
Persistent records and recurrent cues: alter what remains available for future activity.
